## Request

Add a Save button to the settings dialog.

1. It writes settings.json.
2. It shows an error when the write fails.

## Instructions

Read the repository's own instructions (AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md / README) and the code the request touches.

Then draft this task. Acceptance criteria must be observable from outside the code (something a reviewer could check without reading the diff). Verify commands must be the fastest ones that already exist in this repo and actually exercise the criteria -- check package.json scripts, a Makefile, Cargo, or similar before inventing one, and prefer a targeted test over a full CI run. Prefer a test file over a grep check for behaviour. When a command greps for a pattern that may start with `-` (a markdown list item such as `- foo`), put `--` before the pattern: `grep -qF -- '<pattern>' file`. Each verify entry is run verbatim with `sh -c` and must exit 0: only exact shell commands, no prose, no conditions in parentheses. A check that needs judgement (a screenshot, a visual look, "only if X changed") goes into criteria, where the reviewer checks it.

Pick the tier: `mechanical` for a small, fully specified edit, `hard` for work that needs design judgement or touches several subsystems, `standard` otherwise.

When the work changes what a screen shows, the goal must name the exact repo command that produces its screenshot evidence -- look for one before assuming none exists, so the implementer never has to rediscover it. Also put that command in the plan's `screenshot` field: orchd then runs it itself after verify passes and saves the images. Take it only from what the repository already has (package.json scripts, a Makefile, a scripts directory, its own docs); when it has none, leave `screenshot` empty rather than inventing one.

Every `-- check:` must be something this repository can actually run today (its test runner, harness or script exists); do not ask for a kind of test the repo has no harness for.

Ask the owner only about a call that belongs to a person, and only these four kinds: (1) a scope change against the request, (2) money or a paid service, (3) a destructive or irreversible action, (4) the security model or a public API or contract change. Anything else you settle yourself: decide it, fold the decision into the goal, and do not ask. At most 3 questions.

The criteria are the contract the work is judged by. Before writing them, check every factual claim the request makes against the code; when one is wrong, say so in the goal and plan for what is actually true. Write each criterion as `<observable outcome> -- check: <how a read-only reviewer confirms it: a verify command whose output shows it, the file and function to read, or for a visual result the screenshot the implementer must save under artifacts/>`. The reviewer cannot run the app. A criterion whose proof is an image may instead be written as `{"text": "...", "visual": true}`; orchd then requires a saved image under artifacts/ before review. `visual` means the criterion is proven by looking at an image; a criterion checked by a command is never visual, so do not flag one. Mark a criterion visual only for a screen the task changes, name its screenshot file (`artifacts/<name>.png`) in its check, and use one screenshot per changed screen: orchd keeps only the images a visual criterion names as evidence, so the other images a test run leaves under `artifacts/` are dropped.

List in `coverage` every numbered or bulleted item of the request, as its `requirement` text and the 0-based indexes of the `criteria` that prove it; each such item needs at least one criterion with a runnable `-- check:`. A criterion is about the product's behaviour, never about what the agent writes in its report, handoff, summary or decisions.

Give every question a `recommended` option (one of its `options`), the `evidence` for it, and `blocking`: true only when the question is one of the four kinds of call that belong to a person (a scope change against the request, money or a paid service, a destructive or irreversible action, the security model or a public API or contract change). A non-blocking question is not asked: your recommendation is recorded as an assumption and the work goes on, so recommend what you would pick yourself. Blocking questions are asked together in one message.

List in `paths` the repo-relative files or directories the task will edit, as narrowly as you can. Tasks on the same branch never edit one file at once: a task whose paths overlap another running task's waits for it, then continues on top of its landed work. Leave `paths` empty only when you cannot tell.

Search the code with `rg`: it skips .gitignore'd paths such as build output. If `rg` is missing, use `git grep`.

Split the checks by cost. `verify` holds the fast, targeted commands that run after every attempt (a unit test file, the type checker, a linter on the touched paths). `finalVerify` holds the slow whole-repo checks (the full CI script, a desktop smoke) that the orchestrator runs alongside review, after the fast gates pass and before the commit. A subtask's whole-repo checks run at its parent, not in the subtask. Name only commands the repository defines today: read the script names in its package.json (or Makefile, task runner) before you use one, never a script you remember from elsewhere.

For each criterion that a command can prove, add an entry to `checks`: `criterion` is the criterion's 0-based index in `criteria` and `run` a shell command (run with `sh -c` from the repository root, in the task's verify environment). A check must exercise the new behaviour: it must fail on the current code and pass once its criterion is met, and a test that already passes today proves nothing. A check that compares against a branch name (`git diff main`) breaks once the branch moves; compare against the task's base commit with the `ORCHD_BASE_SHA` environment variable instead (`git diff $ORCHD_BASE_SHA`), which orchd sets for every check and verify command. The implementer never commits, so a file it adds is untracked and `git diff` alone never lists it; a check for an added or changed file lists both and greps the path: `{ git diff --name-only $ORCHD_BASE_SHA; git ls-files --others --exclude-standard; } | grep -qx '<path>'`. A check proves behaviour with a test that fails before the change and passes after it, not an exact test name the implementer has to create. A test-name filter that matches zero tests passes, so for tests the plan itself ships use exact test names or assert a count. Leave out a criterion that has no such command. `heldOut` is one optional extra check of the same shape, run after verify; the implementer never sees it, so it may probe what the visible checks do not. The planner session is read-only, so put failing test files in `tests` (`path` repo-relative, `content` the whole file): orchd writes and commits them before the first attempt, and the implementer cannot change them. Tests prove logic, never prose: no test file reads a document (README, docs, guides) to assert its wording. A criterion about a document gets a `checks` command (a grep, a link check) that orchd runs and never commits, and a task that changes only documents ships no test file.

Measurement belongs to orchd's checks. A benchmark, a load test or anything that needs sockets, ports or the network is a check command that orchd runs, never a step the implementer must run, because the implementer's sandbox cannot bind unix sockets. The check produces the before/after numbers itself: it runs the same benchmark on `$ORCHD_BASE_SHA` in a temporary worktree and on the current tree, prints a before/after/delta table, and exits non-zero unless the gain holds. Result files are never committed.

When the request is too large for one agent session, you may split it into `subtasks`, each one agent's session of work. Split only when every part is independently verifiable (its own criteria and verify commands can pass on their own), prefer 2-5 parts, and keep dependent work serial: a part that builds on another lists that part's `key` in its `dependsOn` and starts only after it has landed. Parts that edit the same files belong in one part. List in each part's `paths` the repo-relative files or directories it edits; list in `check` the one targeted command that proves that part alone (or put it first in `verify`). Incomplete parts whose paths overlap, parts that list no paths or parts that have no targeted check are merged into one task with an ordered checklist. Complete drafts with their own criteria and targeted verification may share paths: orchd serialises them and runs compatible overlaps as a relay on one branch, landed once. Draft every part completely, as you would a task of its own: `key`, `title`, `goal`, `criteria` (strings or `{"text": "...", "visual": true}`, as above), `verify`, `finalVerify`, `paths`, `check`, `screenshot` (the repo command that captures the screenshot evidence when the part changes a screen, else empty), `tier` and `dependsOn`. A part with a title, goal, criteria and verify runs as drafted and is not planned again. Each part's `request` is what its own planner drafts from when the draft is incomplete, so keep it self-contained. With subtasks, the top-level title and goal describe the whole, and the top-level verify commands check the combined result, run once after every part has landed. The top-level verify and finalVerify carry the whole-repo checks (the full CI script): they run once on the combined result, so a part's own finalVerify lists only checks for its own part. When the request fits one session, leave `subtasks` out. Draft `checks` and `heldOut` for each part as well, under the same rules as above; their `criterion` indices count that part's own `criteria`, from 0.

## Report format

End your final message with:

```sushi-plan
{"title":"...","goal":"...","tier":"mechanical|standard|hard","criteria":[],"coverage":[{"requirement":"...","criteria":[0]}],"verify":[],"checks":[{"criterion":0,"run":"..."}],"heldOut":{"criterion":0,"run":"..."},"tests":[{"path":"...","content":"..."}],"screenshot":"","finalVerify":[],"paths":["src/..."],"questions":[{"text":"...","options":["...","..."],"risk":[],"defaultOption":null,"recommended":"...","evidence":"...","blocking":false}],"subtasks":[{"key":"a","title":"...","goal":"...","criteria":[],"verify":[],"checks":[{"criterion":0,"run":"..."}],"heldOut":{"criterion":0,"run":"..."},"finalVerify":[],"paths":["src/..."],"check":"...","tests":[{"path":"...","content":"..."}],"screenshot":"","tier":"mechanical|standard|hard","dependsOn":[],"request":"..."}]}
```

`risk` names what a question commits the owner to, from scope (a change against the request), money, destructive, security, public-api (a public API or contract change), push or deploy (empty when none).
